6.text: Chukchee tradition relates the following regarding trade with America: —

7.text: “On the other side of the sea, in a large forest, live ‘the invisible ones.’

8.text: When they come to trade, one can see only the fox and beaver skins which

9.text: they carry in their hands, and it seems as if the peltries move of themselves.

10.text: They come to meet our traders on the border of the forest, and shout, ‘Let

11.text: us trade!’ The traders take a bundle of tobacco and fling it far away.

12.text: ‘Tobacco, tobacco!’ rings through the forest, but nobody is seen. After a

13.text: while a bag filled with fox or beaver skins is flung from the forest. For one,

14.text: bundle of tobacco they will give a bagful of white-fox skins.”

23.text: This armor, made of small pieces of iron with fastenings of narrow leather

24.text: strips, was very common among the Reindeer Chukchee until recently. Even

25.text: now, many individuals preserve their armor out of reverence for its antiquity.

26.text: Besides armor, helmets and greaves were used, all of which are in some

27.text: degree similar to those of Japanese production. The Chukchee, however, are

28.text: not sufficiently skilled in the blacksmith’s art to forge such armor. The only

29.text: place where it could have been made is in the Koryak village of Poiˊtɪn

30.text: (Russian Paren, Парень), the inhabitants of which have for a long time occupied

31.text: themselves with farriery; and the tradition of the southwestern Chukchee points

32.text: in this direction. The question arises, whether the manufacture of this armor

33.text: was really developed only after the arrival of the Russians, especially as the

34.text: wars have decreased since the last half of the eighteenth century.
